KEMi Inaugural Symposium

KEMi Inaugural Symposium

The Kren Engineering-Based Medicine Initiative (KEMi) celebrated its Inaugural Symposium on Thursday, October 22, 2026, at The Lyceum in the Husky Union Building. KEMi brought together faculty, students, industry partners, and leadership from across academia, healthcare, and the broader Pacific Northwest community. This collaboration between the UW School of Medicine and the UW College of Engineering advances engineering-based approaches to medicine, with the ambition of changing how disease is detected, treated, and prevented.

Thursday, October 22, 2026

About the event

The Lyceum (HUB 160)

After an introduction from KEMi Director and Associate Dean Tueng Shen, George and Martina Kren, whose generous support established KEMi, joined by Zoom from Monterey, California, and were welcomed on the big screen with a long round of applause.

More than 240 attendees filled the seats, including faculty from UW, Gonzaga, WSU, Fred Hutch, the Allen Institute, and Seattle Children’s, alongside representatives from Meta, Walmart, Google, Amazon, Boeing, and Philips Medical, as well as biotech leaders, donors, and venture capital representatives.

View the program (opens a new tab)

From the speakers

President Robert J. Jones, joined by Dean Timothy H. Dellit and Dean Nancy L. Allbritton, opened the program, and special guest speaker Representative Suzan DelBene, who represents Washington’s 1st Congressional District, also welcomed attendees. Nobel Laureate in Chemistry Dr. David Baker gave the special remarks on the design of new protein functions using deep learning.

Nancy L. Allbritton, MD, PhD

Dean, UW College of Engineering

“One of the things I like about KEMi is that it’s about building impact, also. It’s about getting your innovation out of the lab and into industry, so that you make a difference in people’s lives.”

Dean, UW School of Medicine
CEO, UW Medicine

Associate Dean for Medical Technology Innovation

Oral presentations

Dr. Ruikang (Ricky) Wang, Dr. Tueng Shen on behalf of Dr. Xu Chen, Dr. Quansan Yang, and Dr. Ramkumar Sabesan then presented four KEMi projects and answered questions from the audience, giving attendees from across disciplines the chance to engage directly with the researchers.

Optical Coherence Tomography as an Accessible Tool for Clinical Investigations

Using light-based eye imaging to help screen for Alzheimer’s disease.

Ruikang (Ricky) Wang, PhD | Bioengineering; Kren Endowed Chair

Doctor Robot (DocBot): Healthcare Engineering with AI & Robotic Technology

An AI-powered platform that brings hospital-level care to patients at home. 

Tueng T. Shen, MD, PhD | Co-PI, presenting on behalf of the project team
PI: Xu Chen, PhD | Mechanical Engineering

Biosensors for Continuous Molecular Monitoring and Early Warning

An ultrasound-readable sensor that gives early warning of preterm birth.

Quansan Yang, PhD | Materials Science & Engineering
Co-PI: Stephen A. McCartney, MD, PhD | Obstetrics & Gynecology

Early Detection of Photoreceptor Dysfunction in Outer Retinal Disease Using Optoretinograph

Imaging individual light-sensing cells in the living eye to detect retinal disease earlier.

Ramkumar Sabesan, PhD | Ophthalmology
Co-PIs: Jennifer Chao, MD, PhD; Debarshi Mustafi, MD, PhD

Poster symposium

The poster symposium opened at lunch and lasted throughout the afternoon. As attendees mingled, they had the opportunity to ask questions not only of the principal investigators but also of the graduate students working on the projects. Many lively conversations took place around the posters, and new relationships began there, on topics ranging from facial imaging to detecting irregular heart rhythm in patients with atrial fibrillation to a real-time machine vision system to assist with emergency intubation.

Integrating Engineering and Rehabilitation Medicine to Improve Healthcare and Assistive Technology Access and Customizability

Jennifer Mankoff, PhD | Co-PI: Heather A. Feldner, PT, PhD, PCS
Presented by Shariphine Agoalikum and Jerry Cao

Real Time Machine Vision to Enhance Emergency Intubation

Nathan White, MD, MS | Co-PIs: Jenq-Neng Hwang, PhD; Richard Utarnachitt, MD, MS

Leveraging the ADDF and EyeACT Datasets to Learn and Predict Dementia Thereby Identifying Dementia Biomarkers

Yue Wu, PhD

Wearable Assist Device to Improve Visual Function Following Restorative Therapy

James A. Kuchenbecker, PhD | Co-PIs: Russell Van Gelder, MD, PhD; Ruikang Wang, PhD

Injectable Biomaterial-Mediated Transplantation of Limbal Fibroblasts for Treatment of Limbal Stem Cell Deficiency

Yuzuru Sasamoto, MD, PhD | Co-PI: Cole DeForest, PhD
Presented by Kosei Suzuki

High-Resolution Facial Imaging for Non-Invasive Detection of Rhythm Irregularities and Perfusion Deficits in Atrial Fibrillation Patients

Nazem Akoum, MD, MS | Co-PI: Ruikang Wang, PhD

Innovation workshops

Alongside the posters, faculty and researchers from the School of Medicine and the College of Engineering gathered with colleagues from partner institutes and industry at six innovation workshop roundtables on neural engineering and rehabilitation, bio-integrated sensing, artificial intelligence, robotics, medical imaging, and programmable medicines for regeneration. Every table took up the same question: “What will health and healthcare look like in 2050, and what do we need to do, and what technologies do we need to leverage, to get there?”

Rehabilitation, Movement & Neural Engineering

Chet Moritz, PhD

Bio-Integrated Sensing: Materials and Devices in and on the Body

Quansan Yang, PhD

AI-Driven Foundational Regenerative Medicine

Hannele Ruohola-Baker, PhD

Robotics, AI & Emergency Medicine

Xu Chen, PhD and Nathan White, MD, MS

Non-Invasive Medical Imaging for Early Systemic Disease Monitoring

Ruikang (Ricky) Wang, PhD and Nazem Akoum, MD, MS

Building the Future of Programmable Medicines for Regeneration

Jennifer Davis, PhD

Closing remarks

Vice Dean Jihui Yang of the College of Engineering gave closing remarks, and the day ended with an informal reception that brought over 90 participants from all tables together for more discussion and networking.

Behind the scenes, KEMi organized the symposium with extensive use of AI agents, which supported tasks from tracking registrations to preparing signage and the printed program, and allowed a small team to plan and run the event. KEMi also relied on dedicated volunteers who welcomed guests, helped with wayfinding and check-in, and took notes at each innovation workshop table, producing detailed summaries that will help launch future discussions within the KEMi community.
